title: The only employer of stone cutters: monopsony hiring compared with a competitive labor market
scenario: Corbie Stone Works (invented) is the only employer of stone cutters in a remote town, so it is a monopsony in that labor market. It sells its stone in a perfectly competitive market and maximizes profit.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled graph of the labor market for stone cutters, showing the labor supply curve, the marginal factor cost curve and the marginal revenue product curve. Show the number of cutters Corbie hires and the wage it pays.

slips.MFC: MRP = MFC gives the number hired; the wage is read down on the labor supply curve.

rubric.point: A correctly labeled graph: Wage and Quantity of labor on the axes; an upward-sloping SL; MFC above SL and steeper; a downward-sloping MRP
accept: W and L on the axes
S or SL, MFC (or MRC) and MRP (or D = MRP) labeled

rubric.point: The quantity hired, QM, where MRP = MFC, and the wage WM read on the SL curve at QM (below the MRP and MFC crossing)
accept: QM from MRP = MFC and WM from labor supply, marked on the axes

parts.sample: Wage is on the vertical axis and Quantity of labor on the horizontal axis. SL slopes up; MFC starts at the same point and rises more steeply, above SL; MRP slopes down. Corbie hires QM, where MRP crosses MFC, and pays WM, found by going straight down from that crossing to SL. QM and WM are marked with dashed lines to the axes.

parts.label: B

slips.MFC: A competitive labor market hires where the wage on labor supply equals MRP; MFC matters only to a monopsony.

parts.prompt: On your graph, show the number of cutters that would be hired, and the wage, if the labor market for stone cutters were perfectly competitive.

rubric.point: The point where MRP crosses labor supply (SL), at a larger quantity of labor and a higher wage than QM and WM
accept: where MRP = SL, to the right of QM and above WM

parts.sample: A perfectly competitive labor market would reach the point where MRP crosses the labor supply curve, SL. That point is at a larger quantity of labor than QM and a higher wage than WM, marked with dashed lines to both axes.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Shade the deadweight loss that results from Corbie hiring fewer cutters than a competitive labor market would.

rubric.point: The triangle between MRP and labor supply from QM to the competitive quantity, fully shaded
accept: the area between MRP and SL from QM to where they cross

parts.sample: The deadweight loss is the triangle between the MRP curve above and the labor supply curve below, from QM out to the quantity where MRP meets SL. Those cutters would add more to revenue than the wage they would accept, but Corbie does not hire them.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain why Corbie's marginal factor cost of labor is greater than the wage it pays.

rubric.point: To hire one more cutter, Corbie must raise the wage it pays to all its cutters, so the added cost is the new cutter's wage plus the raise for every cutter already hired
accept: it must pay a higher wage to everyone to attract one more worker

parts.sample: As the only employer, Corbie faces the upward-sloping labor supply curve. To hire one more cutter it has to offer a higher wage, and it must pay that higher wage to every cutter, not just the new one. So the added cost of the extra cutter, its MFC, is the new wage plus the raise for all the others, which is more than the wage itself.
